courses.title: Calculus II
courses.blurb: Integration techniques, applications of the integral, sequences and series, power/Taylor series, polar and parametric curves, first-order ODEs.

units.title: Integration Techniques
units.summary: Substitution, integration by parts, partial fractions, and trigonometric integrals.

concepts.d: Pick u so du replaces the messy part: ∫ f(g(x)) g'(x) dx = ∫ f(u) du. Look for a function and its own derivative in the integrand.
∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v du. Choose u by LIATE order (Logarithmic, Inverse trig, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential) — u is the first kind you hit.
For ∫ sinᵐx cosⁿx dx: odd power → split off one factor and substitute; both even → use half-angle identities (sin²x = (1−cos2x)/2).
√(a²−x²) → x = a sin θ; √(a²+x²) → x = a tan θ; √(x²−a²) → x = a sec θ. Substitute, integrate, then back-substitute.
Factor the denominator; for each linear factor put A/(x−a), for each irreducible quadratic put (Bx+C)/(x²+…). Solve for A, B, C by matching coefficients or plugging convenient x.
For a definite integral with substitution, either change the limits to u-values (cleanest) or back-substitute and evaluate in x. Never mix x-limits with u-variables.

formulas.e: ∫ u dv = u v − ∫ v du
formulas.note: Choose u by LIATE; the remaining factor is dv.
Use when both exponents are even.
Absolute value matters for negative x.
Drops the radical after an x = a tanθ substitution.

example.problem: Evaluate ∫ x eˣ dx.
steps: Integrate by parts: let u = x, dv = eˣ dx → du = dx, v = eˣ.
Apply ∫u dv = uv − ∫v du: = x eˣ − ∫ eˣ dx.
∫ eˣ dx = eˣ, so the result is x eˣ − eˣ + C = eˣ(x − 1) + C.
Check by differentiating: d/dx[eˣ(x−1)] = eˣ(x−1) + eˣ = x eˣ ✓.
example.answer: ∫ x eˣ dx = eˣ(x − 1) + C.

traps: Choosing u badly in by-parts (pick the LIATE-first factor, not the easy-to-integrate one).
Forgetting + C on every indefinite integral — it costs marks.
Leaving a u-substitution answer in terms of u for an indefinite integral.

practice.q: Evaluate ∫ ln x dx.
practice.a: By parts with u = ln x, dv = dx: = x ln x − ∫ x·(1/x) dx = x ln x − x + C = x(ln x − 1) + C.

practice.q: Evaluate ∫ 2x/(x²+1) dx.
practice.a: u = x²+1, du = 2x dx → ∫ du/u = ln(x²+1) + C.

practice.q: Evaluate ∫ eˣ sin x dx (the 'cyclic' by-parts integral).
practice.a: Apply by parts twice; the original integral reappears. I = eˣ(sin x − cos x)/2 + C. Check by differentiating.

example_hard.problem: Evaluate ∫ x² ln x dx.
steps: By parts with u = ln x (LIATE: log before algebraic) and dv = x² dx.
Then du = (1/x) dx and v = x³/3.
∫ x² ln x dx = (x³/3) ln x − ∫ (x³/3)(1/x) dx = (x³/3) ln x − (1/3)∫ x² dx.
∫ x² dx = x³/3, so the result is (x³/3) ln x − x³/9 + C = (x³/3)(ln x − 1/3) + C.
Check by differentiating: d/dx[(x³/3)ln x − x³/9] = x² ln x + x²/3 − x²/3 = x² ln x ✓.
example_hard.answer: ∫ x² ln x dx = (x³/3)(ln x − 1/3) + C.

units.title: Improper Integrals & Applications
units.summary: Integrals to infinity, areas, volumes of revolution, arc length, and work.

concepts.d: Replace an infinite limit or an infinite discontinuity with a variable and take a limit: ∫₁^∞ f = lim(b→∞) ∫₁^b f. If the limit is finite, it converges; otherwise it diverges.
∫₁^∞ dx/xᵖ converges if p > 1 and diverges if p ≤ 1. The single most useful benchmark for convergence.
A = ∫ (top − bottom) dx, or ∫ (right − left) dy. Sketch first — the roles can swap inside the interval.
Disk/washer about the x-axis: V = π∫ (R² − r²) dx. Shells about the y-axis: V = 2π∫ (radius)(height) dx.
L = ∫ √(1 + (dy/dx)²) dx for y = f(x); equivalently ∫ √((dx/dt)²+(dy/dt)²) dt for parametric curves.
W = ∫ F(x) dx. Variable-force problems: express the force as a function of position first (springs: F = kx; pumping: weight of the slice).

formulas.note: Converges only if the limit is a finite number.
Diverges for p ≤ 1 (including the harmonic p = 1).
R = outer radius from the axis, r = inner.
Shells for a y-axis rotation of a y = f(x) region.
Radians/units consistent.

example.problem: Find the volume of the solid formed by revolving the region under y = x² on [0, 2] about the x-axis.
steps: This is a disk: radius R(x) = y = x², so V = π ∫₀² (x²)² dx = π ∫₀² x⁴ dx.
∫ x⁴ dx = x⁵/5; evaluate 0 to 2: (2⁵ − 0)/5 = 32/5.
Multiply by π: V = 32π/5 ≈ 20.1 cubic units.
example.answer: V = 32π/5 ≈ 20.1 units³.

traps: Forgetting to square the radius in the disk/washer formula.
Using x-limits after a u-substitution without converting them (or back-substituting).
Assuming an improper integral converges — always take the limit and show it is finite.

practice.q: Does ∫₁^∞ dx/x³ converge, and to what?
Find the arc length of y = (2/3)x^(3/2) on [0, 3].
Use cylindrical shells to find the volume when y = 1/x on [1, 3] is revolved about the y-axis.
practice.a: V = 2π∫₁³ x·(1/x) dx = 2π∫₁³ dx = 2π(3−1) = 4π ≈ 12.57 units³. Note the radius is x and the height is 1/x.

example_hard.problem: Evaluate the improper integral ∫₀^∞ x e^(−x) dx.
steps: Replace the infinite limit: ∫₀^b x e^(−x) dx, then let b → ∞.
By parts with u = x, dv = e^(−x) dx: du = dx, v = −e^(−x).
As b → ∞, e^(−b)(b+1) → 0 (exponential beats any polynomial), so the value is 1.
example_hard.answer: ∫₀^∞ x e^(−x) dx = 1 — the integral converges.

units.title: Sequences & Series
units.summary: Convergence, divergence, and the tests that decide them.

concepts.d: A sequence lists terms aₙ; a series is their sum Σaₙ. A series needs the terms' partial sums to approach a finite limit to converge.
If lim aₙ ≠ 0, the series diverges. It can NOT prove convergence (harmonic series has aₙ→0 yet diverges).
Σ arⁿ converges to a/(1−r) when |r| < 1, diverges when |r| ≥ 1.
Σ 1/nᵖ converges if p > 1 (e.g. Σ1/n² converges), diverges if p ≤ 1 (harmonic Σ1/n diverges).
Direct: bound the terms by a known series. Limit comparison: lim (aₙ/bₙ) = L with 0 < L < ∞ → both behave the same.
Ratio: L = lim |aₙ₊₁/aₙ|. If L < 1 converge, L > 1 diverge, L = 1 inconclusive. Root test uses |aₙ|^(1/n) — great for nth powers.
Σ(−1)ⁿaₙ with aₙ decreasing and → 0 converges. Absolute convergence is stronger (converges even ignoring signs).

formulas.note: Diverges when |r| ≥ 1.
L<1 conv, L>1 div, L=1 no conclusion.

formulas.e: If lim aₙ/bₙ = L (0<L<∞), both series behave alike
formulas.note: Compare to a p-series or geometric.
Decreasing AND limit zero — both required.

example.problem: Does Σ_{n=1}^∞ 1/n² converge? What about Σ 1/n?
steps: Σ 1/n² is a p-series with p = 2 > 1 → it converges (its sum is π²/6 ≈ 1.645).
Σ 1/n is the harmonic series: p = 1, the boundary case → it diverges.
Note the nth-term test can't tell them apart (both have aₙ → 0), which is why p-series knowledge matters.
example.answer: Σ1/n² converges (p=2>1); Σ1/n diverges (p=1).

traps: Using the nth-term test to claim convergence — it can only show divergence.
Applying the ratio test and getting L = 1, then stating a conclusion (it's inconclusive).
For an alternating series, checking aₙ→0 but not that the terms decrease.

practice.q: Does Σ (n!/10ⁿ) converge?
practice.a: Ratio test: aₙ₊₁/aₙ = (n+1)/10 → ∞, so L > 1 → diverges.

practice.q: Does Σ (−1)ⁿ/n converge, and absolutely?
practice.a: Converges by the alternating series test (1/n↓0), but only conditionally — Σ1/n diverges, so it is not absolutely convergent.

practice.q: Does Σ (−1)ⁿ/√n converge absolutely, conditionally, or not at all?
practice.a: Alternating series test: 1/√n decreases to 0 → converges. But Σ1/√n is a p-series with p = 1/2 ≤ 1 → diverges. So it converges CONDITIONALLY, not absolutely.

example_hard.problem: Determine whether Σ_{n=1}^∞ n²/2ⁿ converges.
steps: Terms involve both a power n² and an exponential 2ⁿ → ratio test.
L = 1/2 < 1 → the series converges (absolutely).
example_hard.answer: Converges by the ratio test (L = 1/2 < 1).

units.title: Power Series & Taylor Series
units.summary: Representing functions as infinite polynomials — and when that's valid.

concepts.d: Σ cₙ(x−a)ⁿ, centred at a. Converges on an interval |x−a| < R (radius of convergence); test the two endpoints separately.
Apply the ratio test to the series; solve |x−a| < R. Inside a power series can be differentiated and integrated term by term.
f(x) = Σ f⁽ⁿ⁾(a)(x−a)ⁿ/n!. Maclaurin is the special case a = 0.
(1+x)^k = Σ C(k,n) xⁿ for any real k, convergent for |x| < 1; useful for approximations.
The Lagrange error bound |Rₙ| ≤ M|x−a|^(n+1)/(n+1)! bounds the truncation error. Series also give limits and integrals that have no elementary antiderivative.

formulas.note: Taylor about x = a replaces 0 with a.

formulas.e: eˣ = Σ xⁿ/n! = 1 + x + x²/2! + x³/3! + …
formulas.note: Converges for all x (R = ∞).
R = 1; the workhorse for integrating/differentiating series.
M bounds |f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾| on the interval.

example.problem: Write the Maclaurin series for eˣ and use its first three terms to approximate e^0.1.
steps: Every derivative of eˣ is 1 at x = 0, so f⁽ⁿ⁾(0) = 1 and eˣ = Σ xⁿ/n!.
First three terms: 1 + x + x²/2.
The true value is e^0.1 ≈ 1.10517, so the error is under 2×10⁻⁴ — the next term is 0.001/6 ≈ 1.7×10⁻⁴.
example.answer: eˣ = Σ xⁿ/n!; three terms at x = 0.1 give ≈ 1.105 (true 1.10517).

traps: Forgetting to check both endpoints of the convergence interval (R alone doesn't include/exclude them).
Mis-stating a memorised series (sign, exponent, or factorial).
Using a series outside its radius of convergence.

practice.q: Find the Maclaurin series for sin x.
Use 1/(1−x) = Σxⁿ to find the series for 1/(1+x²).
practice.a: Replace x with −x²: 1/(1+x²) = Σ(−1)ⁿx^(2n) = 1 − x² + x⁴ − … for |x| < 1.

practice.q: Use the series for eˣ to approximate ∫₀^{0.5} e^(−x²) dx with three terms, and bound the error.
practice.a: e^(−x²) = 1 − x² + x⁴/2 − … Integrating: x − x³/3 + x⁵/10 at x = 0.5 → 0.5 − 0.041667 + 0.003125 = 0.461458. Next term is −x⁷/42 → magnitude at 0.5 is 7.4×10⁻⁴/… ≈ 1.86×10⁻⁴, which bounds the error.

example_hard.problem: Find the Taylor series for ln(1+x) about 0 and state its radius of convergence.
steps: Ratio test gives |x| < 1; at x = 1 the alternating harmonic converges, at x = −1 the harmonic diverges.
example_hard.answer: ln(1+x) = Σ (−1)^(n−1)xⁿ/n for −1 < x ≤ 1 (radius R = 1).

units.title: Parametric & Polar Curves
units.summary: Curves described by a parameter or by radius and angle.

concepts.d: x = x(t), y = y(t). Eliminate t to get a Cartesian equation where possible, but keep the parametric form for calculus.
dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) (requires dx/dt ≠ 0). L = ∫ √((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²) dt.
x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ; r² = x² + y², tan θ = y/x. A single point has infinitely many (r, θ) pairs.
A = ½ ∫_α^β r² dθ. For the region between two curves, integrate ½(r_outer² − r_inner²).
Circles (r = a, r = 2a cos θ), cardioids (r = a(1 ± cos θ)), rose curves (r = a cos(nθ) with n or 2n petals).
dy/dx = (dr/dθ sin θ + r cos θ)/(dr/dθ cos θ − r sin θ) — or convert to parametric and use dy/dx = (dy/dθ)/(dx/dθ).

formulas.note: Same form as arc length, in t.
The ½ is easy to drop.

formulas.e: x = r cos θ,  y = r sin θ
formulas.note: Also r² = x² + y².

example.problem: Find the area enclosed by the cardioid r = 1 + cos θ.
steps: The cardioid is traced fully for 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π.
A = ½ ∫₀^{2π} (1 + cos θ)² dθ.
Expand: (1 + cos θ)² = 1 + 2cos θ + cos²θ.
Use cos²θ = (1+cos2θ)/2: the integrand averages 1 + 0 + ½ = 3/2 per cycle over 2π, giving ∫ = 3π.
example.answer: Area = 3π/2 ≈ 4.71 square units.

traps: Forgetting the ½ in the polar area formula.
Using the wrong angular bounds (find where the curve closes, or where the petals are traced).
Computing dy/dx where dx/dt = 0 (vertical tangent — handle separately).

practice.q: Convert the polar point (2, π/3) to Cartesian.
Find the arc length of x = t², y = (2/3)t³ for 0 ≤ t ≤ 1.
Find the area inside r = 1 and outside r = 2cos θ.
practice.a: They intersect where 1 = 2cos θ → θ = ±π/3. A = 2·½∫₀^{π/3}(1² − (2cos θ)²) dθ = ∫₀^{π/3}(1 − 4cos²θ) dθ = ∫₀^{π/3}(1 − 2(1+cos2θ)) dθ = ∫₀^{π/3}(−1 − 2cos2θ) dθ. Evaluate: [−θ − sin2θ]₀^{π/3} = (−π/3 − √3/2) − 0 → take the absolute magnitude ≈ 1.913 (2π/3 − √3/2 ≈ 2.094 − 0.866 = 1.228; check bounds) — the standard result is 2π/3 − √3/2 ≈ 1.228.

example_hard.problem: Find the slope dy/dx of the polar curve r = 1 + cos θ at θ = π/2.
steps: Treat as parametric: x = r cos θ = (1+cos θ)cos θ, y = r sin θ = (1+cos θ)sin θ.
dx/dθ = −sin θ(1+2cos θ)? — differentiate directly: x = cos θ + cos²θ → dx/dθ = −sin θ − 2cos θ sin θ = −sin θ(1 + 2cos θ).
y = sin θ + sin θ cos θ → dy/dθ = cos θ + cos²θ − sin²θ = cos θ + cos 2θ.
At θ = π/2: sin = 1, cos = 0 → dx/dθ = −1(1+0) = −1; dy/dθ = 0 + cos π = −1.
example_hard.answer: dy/dx = 1 at θ = π/2 (a 45° upward tangent there).

units.title: Introduction to Differential Equations
units.summary: Separable and first-order linear ODEs — the gateway to modelling.

concepts.d: An equation with a derivative, e.g. dy/dx = f(x, y). Order = highest derivative present. A solution is a function, not a number.
If dy/dx = g(x)h(y), separate: dy/h(y) = g(x) dx, then integrate both sides. This is the most common first type.
y′ + P(x)y = Q(x). Multiply by the integrating factor μ = e^{∫P dx}; then (μy)′ = μQ and integrate.
Use the given y(x₀) = y₀ to pin down the constant of integration — the general solution has a C, the IVP has a number.
dy/dt = ky → y = y₀e^{kt}. k > 0 growth, k < 0 decay; the classic model for populations, radioactive decay, cooling (with Newton's law of cooling).
dy/dx gives the slope at each point; a slope field sketches solution families. Equilibrium solutions are where f(y) = 0.

formulas.note: Split, integrate each side, then solve for y.
Turns y′ + Py = Q into (μy)′ = μQ.
Solve for k from data, then use it.
Solution approaches T_env exponentially.

example.problem: Solve dy/dx = 3x²y, given y(0) = 2.
steps: Separate: dy/y = 3x² dx.
Integrate both sides: ln|y| = x³ + C.
Exponentiate: y = A e^{x³} (where A = e^C).
Apply y(0) = 2: 2 = A e⁰ → A = 2.
example.answer: y = 2 e^{x³}.

traps: Adding C to both sides — one constant is enough (fold it into the solution).
Forgetting to apply the initial condition and leaving the answer with a C.
Dropping the absolute value when a log appears, or mis-exponentiating.

practice.q: Solve dy/dx = x/y.
practice.a: y dy = x dx → y²/2 = x²/2 + C → y² − x² = K (hyperbolas).

practice.q: A population grows at 3%/year from 500. Model and predict after 10 years.
A cup of coffee at 90 °C sits in a 20 °C room. After 10 min it is 65 °C. Find the temperature after 30 min (Newton's law of cooling).

example_hard.problem: Solve the first-order linear ODE y′ + 2y = 4x with y(0) = 1.
steps: Identify P(x) = 2, Q(x) = 4x. Integrating factor μ = e^{∫2 dx} = e^{2x}.
Multiply through: e^{2x}y′ + 2e^{2x}y = 4x e^{2x}, i.e. (e^{2x} y)′ = 4x e^{2x}.
Integrate both sides: e^{2x}y = ∫4x e^{2x} dx.
By parts (u = x, dv = e^{2x}dx): ∫4x e^{2x} dx = 4[x e^{2x}/2 − e^{2x}/4] = 2x e^{2x} − e^{2x} + C.

courses.title: Physics II (Electricity & Magnetism)
courses.blurb: Electric charge and field, Gauss's law, potential and capacitance, DC circuits, magnetism and induction, AC circuits and EM waves.

units.title: Electric Charge, Force & Field
units.summary: Coulomb's law, superposition, and the electric field of point charges and dipoles.

concepts.d: Charge comes in multiples of e = 1.60×10⁻¹⁹ C. Like charges repel, unlike attract. Charge is conserved and quantised.
F = k|q₁q₂|/r², k = 8.99×10⁹ N·m²/C². Force is along the line joining the charges; a vector, so superposition applies component-wise.
E = F/q₀ (force per unit positive test charge). For a point charge, E = kq/r² directed away from +q, toward −q.
Total field = vector sum of individual fields. Field lines start on +, end on −, never cross, and their density indicates strength.
Two equal opposite charges ±q separated by d. Dipole moment p = qd. Far away the field falls off as 1/r³ (faster than a point charge's 1/r²).
E = 0 inside; excess charge sits on the surface; the field just outside is perpendicular to the surface; sharp points concentrate charge.

formulas.note: k = 8.99×10⁹ N·m²/C²; also k = 1/(4πε₀).
Direction away from +q, toward −q.

formulas.n: Force on a charge in a field
formulas.note: Vector: a negative charge feels force opposite E.

example.problem: Two point charges, each +1.0 μC, are 0.10 m apart in vacuum. Find the magnitude of the force between them.
steps: Divide by 0.01: F = 0.899 N.
Both are positive, so the force is repulsive.
example.answer: F ≈ 0.899 N, repulsive (like charges).

traps: Dropping the squared r, or forgetting to convert μC → 10⁻⁶ C.
Treating the force as a scalar and ignoring direction in a multi-charge problem.
Forgetting that the force on a negative charge is opposite to E.

practice.q: What is E at 0.20 m from a +2.0 μC point charge?
practice.a: E = kq/r² = (8.99×10⁹)(2.0×10⁻⁶)/(0.20)² = (1.798×10⁴)/0.04 = 4.49×10⁵ N/C, directed away from the charge.

practice.q: Two +3 nC and one −3 nC charge sit at triangle corners. How do you find the net force on one?
practice.a: Compute each pairwise Coulomb force as a vector, then sum them component-wise — superposition.

practice.q: Two +4.0 nC charges sit at (0,0) and (0.20, 0) m. Find the electric field at (0.10, 0.10) m.
practice.a: By symmetry the x-components cancel and only the y-component adds. r = √(0.10²+0.10²) = 0.1414 m; E per charge = kq/r² = (8.99e9)(4e-9)/0.02 = 1798 N/C. The y-component of each is 1798·(0.10/0.1414) = 1271 N/C, so E_y = 2×1271 = 2.54×10³ N/C upward.

example_hard.problem: Charges +2.0 μC at the origin and −3.0 μC at x = 0.40 m. Find the net force on a +1.0 μC charge at x = 0.10 m.
steps: The +1.0 μC at x = 0.10 is pulled LEFT by the +2.0 μC (like charges) and RIGHT by the −3.0 μC (unlike attract).
Force from the left charge: F₁ = k(2e-6)(1e-6)/(0.10)² = 1.798×10⁻²/0.01 = 1.80 N, to the left (−x).
Distance to the right charge: 0.40 − 0.10 = 0.30 m. F₂ = k(3e-6)(1e-6)/(0.30)² = 2.697×10⁻²/0.09 = 0.30 N, to the right (+x).
Net: 1.80 − 0.30 = 1.50 N, directed toward the origin (−x).
example_hard.answer: F_net = 1.50 N in the −x direction (toward the +2.0 μC charge).

units.title: Gauss's Law
units.summary: Flux and the symmetry trick that makes hard field problems easy.

concepts.d: Φ_E = ∫ E·dA — the 'flow' of field through a surface. For a uniform field and flat area, Φ = E A cos θ.
The net flux through any closed surface equals the enclosed charge over ε₀: ∮E·dA = Q_enc/ε₀. Charges outside contribute zero net flux.
Choose a Gaussian surface matching the symmetry (sphere, cylinder, pillbox) so E is constant and perpendicular on the surface — then E·A = Q_enc/ε₀ solves directly.

concepts.t: Field of a point charge / sphere
concepts.d: Outside any spherically symmetric charge distribution, E = kQ/r² (same as a point charge). Inside a uniformly charged insulating sphere E grows as r; inside a conductor E = 0.
Line charge density λ: E = λ/(2πε₀r), radial. Infinite plane with σ: E = σ/(2ε₀), uniform, directed away from a positive sheet.
The field just outside a conductor is σ/ε₀; a Faraday cage (closed conductor) shields its interior — the basis of electrostatic shielding.

formulas.note: Net flux through any closed surface.
Radial, falls off as 1/r.
Uniform field, independent of distance.
θ = angle between E and the normal.

example.problem: Use Gauss's law to find the field at distance r from an infinitely long line with uniform charge density λ.
steps: Symmetry → E points radially outward and is constant on a cylinder of radius r and length L.
Flux through the curved surface = E(2πrL); the two end caps have zero flux (E parallel to them).
Enclosed charge = λL.
Gauss: E(2πrL) = λL/ε₀ → E = λ/(2πε₀r).
example.answer: E = λ / (2π ε₀ r), directed radially outward for positive λ.

traps: Putting the wrong surface area in the flux (cylinder curved area is 2πrL, not πr²).
Forgetting the end-cap flux is zero (E parallel to the cap normal).
Using Q_enc including charges outside the surface — they contribute zero net flux.

practice.q: What is the field just outside an infinite conducting sheet with surface charge density σ = 4.0 μC/m²?
practice.a: For a conductor the field is E = σ/ε₀ = (4.0×10⁻⁶)/(8.85×10⁻¹²) ≈ 4.5×10⁵ N/C, perpendicular to the surface.

practice.q: A cube encloses a +6 μC charge. What is the net flux?
practice.a: Φ = Q/ε₀ = (6×10⁻⁶)/(8.85×10⁻¹²) ≈ 6.8×10⁵ N·m²/C, independent of the cube size.

practice.q: A point charge sits at one corner of a cube. What is the flux through the OPPOSITE face?
practice.a: The charge at a corner is shared by 8 cubes, so each cube encloses Q/8. Within that cube the three faces meeting at the charge carry zero flux (E ∥ face), leaving the three far faces to share Q/8 equally: each gets Q/48 = Q/(48ε₀)·… flux = Q/(48ε₀)? Careful: flux per far face = (Q/8)/(3) /ε₀ = Q/(24ε₀).

example_hard.problem: A solid insulating sphere of radius R has uniform charge density ρ. Find E for r < R and r > R.
steps: Spherical symmetry → a Gaussian sphere of radius r works in both regions.
Inside (r < R): enclosed charge Q_enc = ρ·(4/3)πr³. Gauss: E(4πr²) = ρ(4/3)πr³/ε₀.
Solve: E = ρr/(3ε₀) — grows linearly with r.
Outside (r > R): Q_enc = ρ(4/3)πR³ = Q_total. Gauss gives E(4πr²) = Q/ε₀ → E = Q/(4πε₀r²) = kQ/r² — same as a point charge.
example_hard.answer: Inside: E = ρr/(3ε₀) (linear). Outside: E = kQ/r² (point-charge). They match at r = R.

units.title: Electric Potential & Capacitance
units.summary: Energy per charge, storing charge, and the fields inside capacitors.

concepts.d: V = U/q — potential energy per unit charge, a scalar. For a point charge V = kq/r; the reference V = 0 is usually at infinity.
W = qΔV; the field does work on a positive charge moving to lower potential. Potential diff = voltage; the volt is a joule per coulomb.
E = −dV/dx (in 1D); the field points 'downhill' in potential. In uniform fields, V = Ed.
Surfaces of constant V are perpendicular to E. No work is done moving a charge along an equipotential.
C = Q/V, unit farad (F). Parallel plates: C = ε₀κA/d (κ = dielectric constant). Capacitors in series add reciprocals; in parallel add directly (opposite of resistors).
U = ½CV² = ½QV = Q²/(2C). The energy sits in the electric field, with energy density u = ½ε₀E².

formulas.note: Scalar sum for multiple charges.
Positive charge moving to lower V gains kinetic energy.
Larger plate area or a dielectric raises C; a bigger gap lowers it.
Also Q²/2C or ½QV.
Opposite of resistors.

example.problem: A parallel-plate capacitor has plates of area 2.0×10⁻³ m² separated by 1.0 mm, with air between them. Find C and the energy stored at 100 V.
steps: Numerator: 1.77×10⁻¹⁴; divide by 1.0×10⁻³: C = 1.77×10⁻¹¹ F ≈ 17.7 pF.

traps: Confusing potential (V, scalar, volts) with potential energy (U, joules).
Mixing up series/parallel rules for capacitors with those for resistors.
Forgetting κ in the dielectric formula, or using mm instead of m for d.

practice.q: A 4 μF and a 6 μF capacitor are in series. Find the equivalent capacitance.
What potential does a +5 nC charge create at 0.30 m?
How much work is needed to move a +3.0 μC charge from a point at 200 V to a point at 50 V?
practice.a: W = qΔV = (3e-6)(50 − 200) = (3e-6)(−150) = −4.5×10⁻⁴ J. Negative means the field does the work — the charge speeds up moving to lower potential.

example_hard.problem: A 4.0 μF capacitor (charged to 12 V) is connected across an uncharged 8.0 μF capacitor. Find the final voltage and the energy lost.
steps: Initial charge: Q = C₁V = (4.0 μF)(12 V) = 48 μC; stored energy U_i = ½C₁V² = ½(4e-6)(144) = 288 μJ.
After connection the capacitors are in parallel, so the charge redistributes: V_f = Q_total/C_total = 48/(4+8) = 4.0 V.
Final energy: U_f = ½C_totalV_f² = ½(12e-6)(16) = 96 μJ.
Energy lost = 288 − 96 = 192 μJ (dissipated as heat/radiation in the connecting wires).
example_hard.answer: V_f = 4.0 V; 192 μJ of the 288 μJ is lost — charge is conserved, energy is not.

units.title: Current, Resistance & DC Circuits
units.summary: Ohm's law, series/parallel networks, power, and Kirchhoff's rules.

concepts.d: I = dQ/dt — charge per second, in amperes. Conventional current is the direction positive charge would flow (opposite the electrons).
V = IR. R = ρL/A: longer/thinner wires resist more. Resistivity ρ depends on material and rises with temperature for metals.
P = IV = I²R = V²/R (watts). A resistor dissipates electrical energy as heat; the form you use depends on what's fixed.
Series: R = R₁ + R₂ + … (same current). Parallel: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + … (same voltage); two in parallel: R = R₁R₂/(R₁+R₂).
A real battery: V_terminal = ε − Ir. The terminal voltage drops under load; ε is the open-circuit EMF.
Junction (current): ΣI_in = ΣI_out. Loop (voltage): the algebraic sum of potential changes around any loop = 0. Two independent rules, any number of loops.

formulas.note: Ohmic only if R is constant.
ρ = resistivity (Ω·m).

formulas.e: P = I V = I² R = V² / R
formulas.note: Watts = joules per second.
Product over sum; result is smaller than either.
Junction rule: ΣI_in = ΣI_out.

example.problem: Find the current through, and power burned by, the resistor in this circuit: a 12 V battery (internal resistance 0.5 Ω) in series with a 5.5 Ω resistor.
steps: Total resistance = internal + external = 0.5 + 5.5 = 6.0 Ω.
Current: I = ε/R_total = 12 / 6.0 = 2.0 A.
Terminal voltage: V = ε − Ir = 12 − (2.0)(0.5) = 11 V.
Power in the 5.5 Ω resistor: P = I²R = (2.0)²(5.5) = 22 W.
example.answer: I = 2.0 A; terminal voltage 11 V; P = 22 W in the resistor (and 2 W lost inside the battery).

traps: Ignoring internal resistance (must add it to the loop total).
Using the parallel rule where the resistors are actually in series (or vice-versa).
Assigning the same current to both branches of a parallel pair — it's the voltage that's equal there.

practice.q: A 3 Ω and a 6 Ω resistor in parallel across a 12 V source: total current?
A 100 W bulb on 120 V — what's its resistance?
A battery reads 9.0 V open-circuit and 8.4 V when delivering 0.60 A. Find its internal resistance and EMF.
practice.a: V = ε − Ir → 8.4 = 9.0 − 0.60r → r = 0.6/0.6 = 1.0 Ω. EMF ε = 9.0 V (the open-circuit reading).

example_hard.problem: Two-loop circuit: a 12 V battery with 2 Ω in series, splitting into a 4 Ω and a 6 Ω branch that rejoin. Find each branch current.
steps: The 4 Ω and 6 Ω are in parallel: R_p = (4·6)/(4+6) = 2.4 Ω.
Total resistance = series 2 Ω + 2.4 Ω = 4.4 Ω → total current I = 12/4.4 = 2.73 A.
Voltage across the parallel pair: V_p = I·R_p = 2.73 × 2.4 = 6.55 V.
example_hard.answer: Total 2.73 A; 1.64 A through the 4 Ω, 1.09 A through the 6 Ω. The smaller resistance carries the larger current.

units.title: Magnetism & Induction
units.summary: Forces on moving charge and wires, fields from currents, and Faraday's law.

concepts.d: F = qvB sin θ; direction from the right-hand rule. Unlike the electric force, it acts only on MOVING charge and is perpendicular to v.
F = I L B sin θ. The force direction follows the right-hand rule for current.
Long straight wire: B = μ₀I/(2πr). Solenoid: B = μ₀nI. The field circles the wire (right-hand grip rule).
∮B·dl = μ₀I_enc — the magnetic analogue of Gauss's law; use it with current symmetry (wire, solenoid, toroid).
Φ = BA cos θ (webers). Flux is the magnetic-field analogue of electric flux and drives induction.
EMF = −N dΦ/dt (Faraday). The minus is Lenz's law: the induced current opposes the change in flux — it always fights the cause.

formulas.e: F = q v B sin θ
formulas.note: Zero if v ∥ B; no work done (force ⊥ v).

formulas.e: F = B I L sin θ
formulas.note: Max when the wire ⊥ B.
μ₀ = 4π×10⁻⁷ T·m/A.
Lenz's minus sign gives the induced current's direction.
n = turns per unit length.

example.problem: A straight wire 0.50 m long carries 4.0 A perpendicular to a 0.30 T magnetic field. Find the force, and the EMF induced if the wire is pulled through the field so the flux changes by 0.60 Wb in 0.20 s (single loop).
steps: Induced EMF: EMF = −N ΔΦ/Δt = −1 × (0.60)/(0.20) = −3.0 V.
The magnitude is 3.0 V; the sign (Lenz) means the induced current opposes the increase in flux.
example.answer: F = 0.60 N; induced EMF magnitude = 3.0 V (direction set by Lenz's law).

traps: Using sin θ where cos θ belongs (F = qvB sinθ, Φ = BA cosθ — different angles).
Forgetting the magnetic force does no work (it is perpendicular to v).
Ignoring Lenz's sign — the magnitude is easy, the direction needs the minus.

practice.q: What is B at 0.05 m from a long wire carrying 10 A?
A 200-turn coil sees flux change 0.02 Wb in 0.10 s. Induced EMF?
A 0.60 m conducting rod slides at 3.0 m/s along rails in a 0.40 T field perpendicular to the plane. Find the motional EMF.

example_hard.problem: A proton (m = 1.67×10⁻²⁷ kg, q = 1.60×10⁻¹⁹ C) moves at 2.0×10⁶ m/s perpendicular to a 0.50 T field. Find the radius of its circular path and the period.
steps: The magnetic force supplies the centripetal force: qvB = mv²/r.
Numerator 3.34×10⁻²¹; denominator 8.0×10⁻²⁰ → r = 0.0418 m ≈ 4.2 cm.
example_hard.answer: r ≈ 4.2 cm; T ≈ 1.3×10⁻⁷ s (the period is independent of speed for a fixed qB/m).

units.title: Inductance, AC Circuits & EM Waves
units.summary: Inductors, RLC behaviour, resonance, and how light emerges from electromagnetism.

concepts.d: A coil resists change in current: EMF = −L dI/dt. Inductance L (henry) depends on geometry; energy stored U = ½LI².
Current grows as I = (ε/R)(1 − e^{−t/τ}) with time constant τ = L/R; it never jumps instantly.
Alternating voltage/current oscillate; V_rms = V_peak/√2. Reactance: X_L = ωL (inductor), X_C = 1/(ωC) (capacitor).
Z = √(R² + (X_L − X_C)²). Resonance when X_L = X_C, i.e. ω = 1/√(LC), at which Z is minimum and current is maximum.
V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p; ideal power is conserved so current steps the other way. Underlies AC power distribution.
Changing E makes B and changing B makes E — self-sustaining electromagnetic waves travelling at c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀) ≈ 3.0×10⁸ m/s, the speed of light.

formulas.note: L in henries; opposes the change in current.
Mirrors ½CV² for a capacitor.
Where X_L = X_C, maximum current in series RLC.
'120 V' mains is an RMS value.

example.problem: A series RLC circuit has L = 20 mH and C = 5.0 μF. Find the resonant frequency.
example.answer: f₀ ≈ 503 Hz — at this frequency the series circuit's impedance is minimum and current is maximum.

traps: Using peak instead of RMS values in power calculations (P = V_rms I_rms).
Forgetting the √ in the resonant-frequency formula, or mixing ω and f.
Treating inductor and capacitor reactances as additive rather than opposite (X_L − X_C).

practice.q: What is the RMS voltage of a 170 V peak AC signal?
A transformer has 100 primary and 500 secondary turns, with 120 V in. Output?
practice.a: V_s = V_p N_s/N_p = 120 × 500/100 = 600 V (a step-up transformer).

practice.q: A transformer steps 120 V down to 12 V. If the secondary delivers 3.0 A, and it is ideal, what is the primary current?
practice.a: Ideal transformer conserves power: V_pI_p = V_sI_s → (120)I_p = (12)(3.0) = 36 → I_p = 0.30 A.

example_hard.problem: An RL circuit has ε = 12 V, R = 6.0 Ω and L = 1.5 H. Find the time constant, the final current, and the current at t = 1τ.
steps: Time constant τ = L/R = 1.5/6.0 = 0.25 s.
Final (steady) current I_max = ε/R = 12/6.0 = 2.0 A.
example_hard.answer: τ = 0.25 s; I_max = 2.0 A; at one time constant I = 1.26 A (63.2% of final).

courses.title: Character, Career and Self Development
courses.blurb: Engineering ethics, professional communication, teamwork, and career readiness.

units.title: Professional Identity & Engineering Ethics
units.summary: What it means to be a professional engineer, and how to reason through an ethical dilemma.

concepts.d: A profession has a code of ethics, a licensure/credentialing path, and a duty to public safety — not just an employer.

Fundamental canons: hold public safety paramount, perform only in your competence, be truthful and objective, act as a faithful agent of each employer, avoid conflicts of interest, enhance the profession's honor.
Utilitarian (greatest good — outcomes), Rights/Duty (respect rights & rules — Kant), Virtue (what would a person of good character do). Most cases look different under each.
The NSPE canon that overrides others: when public safety is at risk, that wins over employer loyalty or profit.
Disclosing wrongdoing. Justified when there is serious harm, you have exhausted internal channels, and you have documented evidence. A near-universal sign-on to every code.
Disclose, recuse, or get written approval. Never let a personal interest quietly steer a technical judgement.

formulas.e: Compare Σ Benefits − Σ Harms for each option
formulas.note: Quantify only to compare; the hard part is valuing safety and lives honestly.

formulas.e: Ask: does the action respect the rights of all stakeholders?
formulas.note: Kant: would you accept this as a universal rule?

formulas.e: Would I be comfortable if this decision were public?
formulas.note: A quick smell test for conflicts of interest.

example.problem: A supervisor tells you to sign off on a structural weld you believe is undersized because the inspection deadline is today. What do you do?
steps: Identify stakeholders: public/users (safety), employer (schedule/reputation), you (job, license, integrity).
Framework check — utilitarian: risk of failure (serious harm) outweighs a schedule delay. Rights: users have a right to safe structures. Virtue: a competent engineer does not falsify a judgement.
NSPE canon: public safety is paramount — it overrides the deadline pressure.
Action: do not sign; document the concern in writing; propose a fix (re-weld, re-inspect) and escalate to the next level if refused.
example.answer: Refuse to sign, document in writing, propose remediation, escalate. Safety > schedule; your licence and the public depend on an honest technical call.

traps: 'Just following orders' — acting under instruction is NOT a defence for a professional judgement.
Choosing one framework and ignoring the others: state which you used and why.
Treating ethics as opinion — the codes and canon give a defensible standard.

practice.q: A vendor offers you free equipment for your lab if you recommend their product. Which canon applies?
practice.a: Conflict of interest — disclose it and recuse from the recommendation; free goods must not steer a technical judgement.

practice.q: Which NSPE canon overrides the rest when they conflict?
practice.a: Hold paramount the safety, health, and welfare of the public.

practice.q: Give the three frameworks and one case where they disagree.
practice.a: Utilitarian, rights, virtue. A bridge-cost cut that harms a few but saves money: utilitarian may favour the cut; rights/virtue object.

practice.q: Your manager asks you to omit a known failure mode from a report to a regulator, saying 'it's not material'. How do you respond?
practice.a: Refuse to omit it. Frame it as a professional and legal exposure, not a personal objection: misrepresenting a known hazard to a regulator breaches the paramount-safety canon and can be fraud. Offer to document the risk with mitigations so the report is complete AND constructive; escalate if pressed.

example_hard.problem: You discover a colleague signed off on test results that were never run, and a product is about to ship. Analyse fully.
steps: Stakeholders: the public (safety), your employer (liability/reputation), the colleague (job), you (job, licence, duty).
Utilitarian: shipping untested product risks serious harm — the expected harm outweighs the schedule or loyalty benefit.
Rights/duty: users have a right not to be exposed to an untested hazard; NSPE places public safety paramount.
Virtue: a person of good character does not stay silent to protect a colleague.
Action ladder: verify your understanding → raise it directly and privately → escalate to the supervisor → document in writing → escalate further / regulator if unresolved.
example_hard.answer: Escalate with written documentation, starting privately, and continue up the chain if unresolved — the untested sign-off is falsified data, not a judgement call, and public safety outranks loyalty.

units.title: Technical Communication
units.summary: Writing and presenting engineering work so a decision-maker can act on it.

concepts.d: Before writing, name the reader: technical peer, manager (wants decisions/cost), or public (wants plain language). Same facts, different framing.
Engineering reports lead with the conclusion/recommendation, then evidence, then method. Busy readers stop after the first paragraph.
One page: problem, what you did, key result, recommendation/next step. Written last, read first.
Every figure needs a number, a caption, and an in-text reference. Axis labels carry units. A figure the reader can't read is a defect.
Active voice, short sentences, one idea per sentence, define jargon on first use, no nominalisations ('utilise' → 'use').
Tell them what you'll say, say it, tell them what you said. One message per slide; slides support you, not the reverse.

formulas.note: Reverse of how most people write. Reorder after drafting.
If it doesn't fit, it belongs in the appendix or a handout.

example.problem: Rewrite for a busy plant manager: 'An investigation of the failure modes of the pump was undertaken and it was determined that cavitation was the causative mechanism.'
steps: Find the recommendation/result: the pump failed by cavitation.
Lead with it; drop passive voice and nominalisations.
Keep the evidence available below: NPSH margin too low, impeller erosion pattern.
example.answer: 'The pump failed by cavitation. The cause is a low NPSH margin at high flow.' — result first, mechanism second, evidence in the body.

traps: Burying the conclusion on page 8 — the manager never gets there.
Unlabelled axes or a missing unit — makes the figure meaningless and loses trust.
Slides with paragraphs — the audience reads instead of listening.

practice.q: What goes in the first sentence of an engineering memo?
practice.a: The conclusion or recommendation (inverted pyramid).

practice.q: Name three checks for a good technical figure.
practice.a: Numbered + captioned, axes labelled with units, referenced in the text.

practice.q: Critique this figure caption: 'Fig 3. Results.'
practice.a: It fails on every count: no figure number convention issue but no description of what is plotted, no axes/units statement, no takeaway, and no in-text reference. A good caption reads what is shown, the conditions, and the key result — e.g. 'Figure 3. Pump efficiency vs. flow rate at 25 °C. Efficiency peaks at 68% near 40 L/min.'

example_hard.problem: A 12-page report buries its recommendation on page 11. Restructure it and explain the changes.
steps: Identify the single most important sentence (the recommendation) and everything supporting it.
Apply the inverted pyramid: executive summary with problem → finding → recommendation → cost/next step.
Move the detailed method and raw data to appendices; keep evidence for the recommendation in the body.
Number and caption every figure, reference each in the text, and label axes with units.
Cut nominalisations and passive voice: 'an evaluation was undertaken' → 'we evaluated'.
example_hard.answer: Lead with the recommendation in a one-page executive summary, keep supporting evidence in the body, move method/raw data to appendices, and rewrite in active voice — the reader must be able to act after the first page.

units.title: Teamwork, Leadership & Conflict
units.summary: How engineering teams form, why they fight, and how to resolve it cheaply.

concepts.d: Forming → Storming → Norming → Performing (→ Adjourning). Conflict in Storming is normal, not failure.
Effective teams cover nine behaviours (Plant, Coordinator, Shaper, Monitor-Evaluator, Implementer, Completer-Finisher, Resource Investigator, Teamworker, Specialist). Gaps cause predictable failure.
Competing, Collaborating, Compromising, Avoiding, Accommodating — chosen by assertiveness × cooperativeness. Collaborate for important + trust; avoid only for trivial.
Situation–Behaviour–Impact. Describe observable behaviour and its effect; avoid character judgements.
A shared belief it's safe to speak up. It is the strongest predictor of team learning; build it with questions, not blame.

formulas.note: Assertive + cooperative quadrant.

formulas.e: In <situation>, when you <behaviour>, the impact was <impact>
formulas.note: Behaviour = observable; impact = effect, not judgement.

example.problem: A teammate keeps missing deadlines, and the team is falling behind. Your report is due tomorrow.
steps: Diagnose stage: this is Storming pressure, not yet a people problem.
Use SBI privately: 'At the last two stand-ups (S), the design file wasn't updated (B), which blocked my analysis (I).'
Choose a mode: Collaborating — the relationship and the deadline both matter.
Agree a concrete change (smaller, earlier checkpoints) and a review date.
example.answer: Private SBI conversation, collaborative mode, agree a concrete checkpoint change and follow up — do not escalate or absorb the work silently.

traps: Avoiding conflict to 'keep the peace' — it reappears worse at the deadline.
Feedback that attacks the person ('you're lazy') instead of the behaviour.
Escalating before trying a direct, respectful conversation.

practice.q: Which conflict mode fits a trivial issue you'll never see again?
practice.a: Avoiding (or Accommodating) — low importance, low stakes.

practice.q: Expand SBI and give one example.
practice.a: Situation–Behaviour–Impact. e.g. 'In stand-up today, when you cut the checklist step, it worried the client.'

practice.q: A quiet team member's correct objection is being ignored in design meetings. What do you do as the lead?
practice.a: Protect psychological safety explicitly: name the objection, ask the person to expand, and record it in the decision log. If the team still overrides it, require the decision record to state WHY it was overridden — this makes dissent safe and traceable, and often changes the outcome.

example_hard.problem: One teammate has stopped contributing; the other two are resentful and the deadline is in a week. Diagnose and act.
steps: Diagnose the Tuckman stage: this is Storming pressure surfacing as resentment — normal, not terminal.
Check your assumptions first: is it capability, capacity, clarity, or motivation? Different causes, different fixes.
Hold a private SBI conversation: 'At the last two stand-ups (S), the model file wasn't updated (B), which blocked my part (I).'
Choose Collaborating in Thomas-Kilmann — both the relationship and the deadline matter.
Agree a concrete, small, earlier checkpoint and re-split the remaining work explicitly; set a review date.
example_hard.answer: Private SBI conversation to find the real cause, Collaborating mode, then re-contract with smaller checkpoints — and escalate only if a documented agreement is broken, not to 'fix' the person.

units.title: Career Readiness
units.summary: Résumés, interviewing, and the path from student to licensed engineer.

concepts.d: One page: contact, education, relevant experience/projects (bulleted, results first), skills, leadership. No photo, no 'references on request'.
Situation–Task–Action–Result. Lead with a strong verb and quantify the result ('Cut model-prep time 30% by scripting a macro').
Interviewers ask for stories ('tell me about a conflict'); answer with STAR, keep it 90 seconds, end on the result/lesson.
Applicant Tracking Systems parse your file: mirror the job's keywords, use a simple single-column layout, avoid tables/graphics columns.
ABET degree → FE exam (Fundamentals of Engineering, often senior year) → ~4 years supervised experience → PE exam. FE/PE matter for public-works and consulting roles.
Most roles are filled through people. Send a specific thank-you within 24 h referencing something you discussed.

formulas.note: Every résumé bullet and interview answer follows this shape.

formulas.e: Strong verb + what you did + measurable result
formulas.note: 'Reduced X by Y% by doing Z.'

example.problem: Turn 'worked on a bridge project' into a résumé bullet.
steps: Name the task and your specific action, not the team's.
Add a number if you can (scope, cost, time, %).
Lead with the strongest verb; keep to one line.
example.answer: “Modelled a 40-ft pedestrian bridge in CAD; cut drawing revision cycles 25% by building a parametric assembly.”

traps: Duties instead of results — 'responsible for' tells the reader nothing.
A two-column template that ATS software mangles; you never get seen.
No follow-up after the interview — a large share of offers are won there.

practice.q: What do the letters FE and PE stand for and when do you take them?
practice.a: Fundamentals of Engineering (typically near graduation) and Principles and Practice of Engineering (after ~4 years supervised experience).

practice.q: Give the STAR expansion and what each part must contain.
practice.a: Situation (context), Task (your goal), Action (what YOU did), Result (measurable outcome/lesson).

practice.q: Rewrite for ATS and impact: 'Responsible for helping with various engineering tasks on team projects.'
practice.a: Strip the duty language and add scope + result: 'Modelled and toleranced 12 machined parts across 3 team projects; cut drawing revision cycles 25% by building a parametric CAD library.' Mirror the job posting's keywords (CAD, tolerancing, DFM) and keep it one line.

example_hard.problem: Build a STAR answer to 'Tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate.'
steps: Situation (15s): set the context — a 4-person design project, two weeks out.
Task (10s): you needed an agreed material choice to finish the analysis.
Action (45s): you asked for the reasoning, built a weighted comparison of the two options, presented data in a joint review, and proposed a test to settle it.
Result (20s): the team chose the alternative on the evidence; you delivered on time and the part passed the later test.
Then stop — do not ramble. Land the result and the lesson.
example_hard.answer: Situation → Task → Action → Result, ending on the measurable outcome and what you'd repeat. Keep it ~90 seconds, and use 'I' for your actions, not 'we' for everything.

units.title: Self-Management & Growth Mindset
units.summary: The habits that keep a heavy engineering load from crushing you.

concepts.d: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound. 'Do better in statics' is not a goal; 'finish 10 practice problems per unit before each quiz' is.
Sort by urgency × importance. Spend time in Quadrant II (important, not urgent): studying early, sleep, exercise.
Study in 50-minute focus blocks with phones out of the room. Multitasking raises mistakes on problem sets.
Ability grows with effort and strategy. 'I can't do statics' → 'I haven't found the right method yet.' Effort + feedback = learning.
After each exam: what worked, what failed, one change next time. A 10-minute review beats another hour of aimless reading.

formulas.note: Test every goal against all five.

formulas.e: Q1 urgent+important (do) · Q2 not-urgent+important (schedule) · Q3 urgent+not-important (delegate) · Q4 neither (delete)
formulas.note: Win by living in Q2.

example.problem: You have a statics quiz in 5 days and keep cramming the night before. Build a plan.
steps: SMART goal: 'Complete the truss and friction practice sets (10 problems each) by Day 3, and a full mock quiz on Day 4.'
Place in Q2: schedule 50-minute blocks Days 1-3 in your calendar, not 'when I get to it'.
Active recall: redo problems closed-book, then check; flashcards for formulas.
Reflect after the quiz: note the two topics that cost the most marks; target them next cycle.
example.answer: Schedule Q2 focus blocks, do closed-book practice sets (not re-reading), then a timed mock quiz, then a short reflection to retarget.

traps: Confusing busy with productive — highlighting a textbook is not studying.
All-night cramming: recall collapses within days; spaced practice wins.
Setting a vague goal you can never tell you've met.

practice.q: Which Eisenhower quadrant should most study time live in, and why?
practice.a: Quadrant II (important, not urgent) — that's where prevention and real learning happen.

practice.q: Rewrite 'study more' as a SMART goal.
practice.a: e.g. 'Finish 12 statics practice problems per week, tracked in a log, through the end of the term.'

practice.q: You scored 55% on a quiz you studied 8 hours for. Run the reflection loop.
practice.a: Separate process from content: what method did the 8 hours use (re-reading?), what topics cost marks, what question types failed (recall vs multi-step)? Then change ONE thing next cycle — typically switch from re-reading to closed-book practice and add spaced review — and re-measure on the next quiz.

example_hard.problem: You have two exams in 6 days and a lab report due in 3. Build an executable plan.
steps: Write SMART goals for each: 'Lab report submitted Day 3'; '80% on both mock exams by Day 5'.
Place the work in Eisenhower Q2: schedule 50-minute blocks now, not 'when I get to it'.
Order by urgency × importance: lab report (Day 3) blocks first; interleave exam topics in spaced blocks.
Use active recall only: closed-book practice problems and self-quizzing, not re-reading.
Schedule a review slot each night for the day's errors, and protect sleep — recall consolidates in sleep.
example_hard.answer: SMART goals, Q2 calendar blocks, urgency-ordered, active recall with nightly error review, sleep protected. A plan you can execute beats a plan that lists everything.

courses.title: Modeling and Design
courses.blurb: The engineering design process, visualization, CAD solid modeling, and engineering drawings.

units.title: The Engineering Design Process
units.summary: From a vague need to a justified concept choice.

concepts.d: Analysis has one right answer given assumptions; design has many defensible answers and needs a rationale. You justify, you don't 'solve'.
Write the need as a problem statement plus a requirements list: functional (what it must do) and constraints (limits: budget, size, safety codes).
Break the top function into sub-functions (e.g. 'transmit torque' → 'couple input', 'reduce speed', 'seal lubricant'). Each sub-function gets its own concepts.
Diverge before you converge: brainstorm, morphological analysis (combine sub-solution options), reverse-engineer, benchmark competitors.
Score concepts against weighted criteria; a datum concept anchors the scale (−1/0/+1 or 1-5). Choose the highest weighted total; document why.
Design is a loop: define → concept → model → test → revise. A design review is a scheduled, documented checkpoint with fresh eyes.

formulas.note: Weights must sum to 1 (or 100%). Keep units consistent.

formulas.e: Datum concept = all zeros; others scored relative to it
formulas.note: Forces you to define 'good' once.

example.problem: Pick a bicycle frame material among steel, aluminium, and carbon using a Pugh matrix. Criteria weights: cost 0.35, weight 0.30, strength 0.20, repairability 0.15. Scores (1-5): steel 5/2/4/5, alu 4/3.5/3.5/3, carbon 1/5/5/1.
steps: Highest score wins; sensitivity-check by nudging the top weights.
example.answer: Steel = 3.90, Aluminium = 3.60, Carbon = 3.00 → steel wins under these weights. Always state the weights and note that changing them can flip the result.

traps: Jumping to a concept before writing requirements — you can't justify what you didn't define.
Weights that don't sum to 1 (or 100%) → scores are meaningless.
Treating the matrix as objective truth: it makes assumptions explicit, it doesn't remove judgement.

practice.q: What's the difference between a functional requirement and a constraint?
practice.a: Functional = what the design must DO (transmit torque). Constraint = a limit on the solution (budget, envelope, code).

practice.q: Why keep a datum concept in a Pugh matrix?
practice.a: It anchors the scale so every other concept is judged against one known baseline.

practice.q: Functionally decompose a 'portable phone charger' down to three sub-functions, then name a concept for each.
practice.a: Sub-functions: (1) store energy → battery cell chemistry (Li-ion vs Li-polymer); (2) convert/regulate voltage → boost converter IC vs charge-pump; (3) interface to the phone → USB-C receptacle vs wireless coil vs pogo pins. Each sub-function has its own concept choice, recombined by morphological analysis.

example_hard.problem: Run a full Pugh matrix for a phone stand: criteria cost 0.30, portability 0.25, stability 0.25, aesthetics 0.20. Concepts: folded card, hinged plastic, 3D-printed wedge. Datum = hinged plastic (all 0). Card: cost +2, portability +2, stability −2, aesthetics −1. Wedge: cost −1, portability 0, stability +2, aesthetics +1.
steps: Hinged plastic is the datum → score 0 everywhere (total 0).
Tie — run a sensitivity check: raise the stability weight to 0.35 (and cut aesthetics to 0.10).
Recompute: card = 0.60 + 0.50 − 0.70 − 0.10 = +0.30; wedge = −0.30 + 0 + 0.70 + 0.10 = +0.50 → the wedge wins on stability-led weighting.
example_hard.answer: Tie at +0.40 each; the decision hinges on how much you weight stability. State the weights you used — a matrix makes assumptions explicit, it does not produce certainty.

units.title: Visualization & Sketching
units.summary: Reading and drawing the shapes that describe a part.

concepts.d: Front, top, right-side views arranged in standard (third-angle, US) positions. Each view shows two of the three dimensions — together they define the shape.
All three axes at 120°; true lengths along the axes. Great for 'what does it look like', poor for dimensions.
Visible = thick solid; hidden = dashed; centre = chain; and the rule 'no hidden lines in section views'.
Cut the part to show internal features; hatch the cut material. Full, half, and offset sections each reveal different internals.
Auxiliary views show a true shape on an angled face; detail views enlarge a busy region with its own scale.

formulas.e: Front (centre) · Top (above front) · Right side (right of front)
formulas.note: US standard. First-angle (EU) mirrors the top/side.

formulas.e: Three axes 120° apart; vertical axis true-vertical
formulas.note: Circles become ellipses on the isometric planes.

example.problem: You see one view: a rectangle with a hidden dashed square in the middle and a centreline. What feature is hidden and in what direction?
steps: Dashed line = hidden edge → the feature is behind the visible face.
Centreline through it = a symmetric feature, typically a hole or slot.
Need at least one other view to fix depth and shape.
example.answer: A symmetric hidden internal feature (commonly a through-hole) perpendicular to that face; the second view locks the shape and depth.

traps: Drawing hidden lines in a section view — wrong by convention.
Mixing first- and third-angle placement on one sheet.
Assuming one view defines a part — it never does.

practice.q: What does a dashed line mean, and when is it omitted?
practice.a: A hidden (obscured) edge; omitted in section views.

practice.q: Which view type shows an angled face at true size?
practice.a: An auxiliary view.

practice.q: Why must hidden lines be omitted in a section view, and what replaces them?
practice.a: A section view shows the interior directly, so hidden (obscured) edges are no longer hidden — drawing them would be wrong by convention and would clutter the view. They are replaced by the visible solid edges of the cut, plus hatching on the cut material to distinguish it from background material.

example_hard.problem: You have a front view showing a rectangle with a solid circle in the middle and a side view showing a rectangle with a hidden dashed rectangle behind the front plane. Describe the part.
steps: The front view's solid circle means a through-feature is visible from the front — likely a hole or boss along the front-to-back axis.
The side view's hidden dashed rectangle sits behind the front face → an internal cavity or counterbore, not visible from the side.
Cross-reference: the circle diameter must match the hidden rectangle's height in the side view.
Because the hidden feature is a rectangle (not a circle) in the side view, the cavity is not round in that plane — it is a rectangular pocket, or the hole is drilled into a rectangular recess.
Conclusion needs a third view or a section view to fix the depth and shape.
example_hard.answer: A round through-feature on the front face leading into a rectangular internal cavity (pocket/counterbore). Two views define most of the shape; a section view is required to confirm depth and the pocket shape.

units.title: CAD & Solid Modeling
units.summary: Parametric features, sketches, and assemblies — how modern parts are built.

concepts.d: A model is a history of features (sketch → extrude → fillet → pattern). Edit an early sketch and later features rebuild — that's the power and the fragility.
A sketch is 'black' when all degrees of freedom are removed by dimensions/relations; blue = under-constrained. Always fully constrain before extruding.
Coincident, horizontal/vertical, parallel/perpendicular, tangent, equal, symmetric, concentric. Relations encode design intent so edits behave predictably.
Extrude (linear), revolve (about an axis), sweep (profile along a path), loft (blend between profiles), hole, fillet/round, chamfer, shell, pattern/mirror.
Mates remove degrees of freedom: coincident, concentric, distance, angle, tangent. Count DOF to see if an assembly is over- or under-constrained (a part has 6 DOF).
Model so the features you expect to change are the easiest to change. Name features; avoid references to geometry you might delete.

formulas.note: Fully define a part when constrained mates = 0 remaining DOF.

formulas.e: Total instances = count × (1 + number of directions)
formulas.note: Watch for overlapping instances in linear/circular patterns.

example.problem: A bracket must have 4 bolt holes equally spaced on a 100 mm bolt circle. Describe the efficient CAD method.
steps: Sketch one hole on the bolt circle, dimension its position (e.g. on the X-axis at R = 50 mm).
Use a Circular Pattern feature: axis = centre, angle = 360°, count = 4, equal spacing.
Fully constrain the base sketch first so a diameter change rebuilds cleanly.
example.answer: One hole feature + circular pattern (count 4, 360°) about the centre axis — never 4 hand-placed holes (unmaintainable).

traps: Extruding an under-constrained (blue) sketch — the model drifts when edited.
Over-constraining with redundant dimensions → solver errors you can't fix.
Referencing a fillet face that a later edit deletes → broken rebuild.

practice.q: How many degrees of freedom does a free body have in 3D?
practice.a: Six: three translations and three rotations.

practice.q: What does it mean when a sketch turns black and why does it matter?
practice.a: It is fully constrained — all DOF removed; safe to extrude and stable under edits.

practice.q: An assembly has 3 parts and 14 mates defined, but the parts still move. Diagnose.
practice.a: Count degrees of freedom: each free rigid body has 6, so 3 parts = 18 DOF. Mates must remove all but the assembly's global 6 (or fully fix one part). 14 mates may include redundant mates on already-fixed DOF and still leave one axis free — typical culprits are a missing concentric or a coincident that only locks one rotation. Add the specific missing DOF constraint rather than more mates.

example_hard.problem: A symmetric bracket needs 4 holes on a 100 mm bolt circle AND mirrored stiffening ribs on both sides. Describe an efficient, robust CAD strategy.
steps: Fully constrain the base sketch first (black sketch) so later parameters rebuild predictably.
Create ONE hole as a feature positioned on the bolt circle at a defined angle.
Use a Circular Pattern on that hole: axis = centre, angle 360°, count 4, equal spacing.
Create ONE rib feature on a plane at the symmetry centre; then Mirror the rib about the part's mid-plane rather than drawing a second rib.
Order matters: place fillets AFTER patterns/mirrors so edges exist to fillet; name every feature for maintainability.
example_hard.answer: Fully-constrained base sketch → one hole + circular pattern → one rib + mirror about the mid-plane → fillets last. Two 'source' features create eight real ones and a rebuild that survives edits.

units.title: Engineering Drawings & Tolerances
units.summary: Turning a 3D model into a manufacturing document.

concepts.d: Dimension to a feature once, from datums, never duplicate, and never dimension to a hidden line if avoidable. Dimensions carry units and the required precision.
A dimension without a tolerance is undefined. Clearance fit (hole larger), interference fit (shaft larger), transition (either).
Limits give the two extreme sizes directly; bilateral (±) is symmetric; unilateral applies one side (common for holes).

Geometric tolerancing controls form (flatness, straightness), orientation (perpendicularity), location (position/true position), and runout. Read a feature control frame: symbol | tolerance | datum(s).
Ra (µm) specifies roughness; the title block holds part number, material, scale, revision, and who approved.

formulas.note: MMC/LMC shift the band for geometric controls.
Applies to a hole located by rectangular coordinates.

example.problem: A Ø10 mm hole is dimensioned 10.00 / 10.05 mm. Classify the fit against a shaft made 9.98 / 9.99 mm, and state the allowance.
steps: Hole range 10.00-10.05; shaft range 9.98-9.99.
The hole is always larger than the shaft (10.00 > 9.99) → clearance fit.
Allowance = minimum clearance = hole min − shaft max = 10.00 − 9.99 = 0.01 mm.
Maximum clearance = hole max − shaft min = 10.05 − 9.98 = 0.07 mm.
example.answer: Clearance fit; allowance (min clearance) = 0.01 mm, max clearance = 0.07 mm.

traps: Over-dimensioning (same feature twice) → contradictory tolerances, rejected by the shop.
Leaving a dimension untoleranced — the machinist then invents one.
Reading a feature-control frame left-to-right wrongly; the datum order changes the meaning.

practice.q: Define 'allowance' in a fit.
practice.a: The intentional difference between the sizes of mating parts — minimum clearance (or maximum interference).

practice.q: What are the four GD&T control families?
practice.a: Form, orientation, location, and runout.

practice.q: Explain why a hole dimensioned 10.00/10.05 with a shaft at 9.98/9.99 is a clearance fit, and give both clearances.
practice.a: The hole is always larger than the shaft (10.00 > 9.99), so clearance always exists. Minimum clearance = 10.00 − 9.99 = 0.01 mm; maximum clearance = 10.05 − 9.98 = 0.07 mm. The allowance (intentional minimum) is 0.01 mm.

example_hard.problem: A 4-hole pattern on a 200 mm square is specified with position tolerance Ø0.5 MMC at LMC datum. Holes are Ø12.00/12.20; the mating studs are Ø11.90/11.95. Compute the MMC bonus tolerance and the resulting clearance range.
steps: MMC of the hole = smallest permitted hole = 12.00 mm. Bonus tolerance = actual size − MMC.
At the largest hole (12.20) the bonus is 12.20 − 12.00 = 0.20 mm, added to the Ø0.5 position tolerance → Ø0.70 allowed.
Clearance = hole size − stud size. Minimum clearance (worst case): smallest hole 12.00 − largest stud 11.95 = 0.05 mm — but the position tolerance erodes this.

Effective minimum clearance with position error: 0.05 − (0.5/2 on each side) — for a Ø tolerance zone, subtract the full radial allowance: 0.05 − 0.5 = −0.45 mm at MMC (i.e. interference is possible).
At LMC with bonus: clearance available = (12.20 − 11.90) = 0.30 mm plus the 0.20 mm bonus → far more forgiving.
example_hard.answer: Bonus tolerance at LMC = 0.20 mm (zone grows Ø0.5 → Ø0.70). At MMC the 0.05 mm clearance is smaller than the position zone, so interference is possible — tighten the size limits or loosen the position callout.

units.title: Design for Manufacturing & Prototyping
units.summary: Designs that are cheap and easy to build — and how to test them fast.

concepts.d: Design for Manufacturing = easy to make (few operations, standard tools). Design for Assembly = few parts, self-aligning, one-direction insertion. Both cut cost dramatically, and cheapest to apply at concept stage.
Cost rises steeply as tolerances tighten. Specify the loosest tolerance the function allows — not the tightest the machine can hold.
Match the design to a process: casting (complex, high volume), machining (accurate, low-moderate), injection moulding (high volume plastics, needs draft), sheet metal (thin, cheap).
3D printing (FDM/SLA/SLS) builds from a model in hours — ideal for form/fit checks. Weak in the build direction and anisotropic; reinforce or use it as a fit check only.
Worst-case: sum the individual tolerances. Statistical (RSS): √(Σ tolᵢ²). RSS explains why most assemblies fit even when worst-case says they shouldn't.

formulas.note: Guarantees assembly for every part; conservative.
Realistic for large volumes if the distributions are centred.

example.problem: A stack of 3 parts has tolerances ±0.2, ±0.1, ±0.15 mm. Find worst-case and RSS total gap tolerance.
steps: Compare against the allowed gap and pick the method your production volume justifies.
example.answer: Worst-case = 0.45 mm; RSS ≈ 0.269 mm. RSS is tighter because random errors partially cancel.

traps: Tightening tolerances to fix a problem it wasn't causing — cost explodes, real cause remains.
Using an FDM print to check a sliding fit at full size — build shrink/anisotropy misleads you.
Designing for one-off prototype methods when the product needs high-volume production.

practice.q: When is RSS tolerance stackup appropriate vs. worst-case?
practice.a: RSS for high-volume production where per-part errors are independent and centred; worst-case when every assembly must fit (low volume, safety-critical).

practice.q: Why is DFM best applied at the concept stage?
practice.a: Cost is locked in early; changing a concept is cheap, changing a shipped design is not.

practice.q: A part is failing fit checks and a colleague proposes halving all tolerances. Critique this.
practice.a: It treats the symptom and multiplies cost — cost rises steeply as tolerances tighten and the real cause is likely elsewhere (a datum error, a stackup not analysed, or a process capability issue). Diagnose first: compute the actual stackup (worst-case vs RSS), measure the process capability (Cpk), and tighten only the contributor that actually consumes the budget.

example_hard.problem: A 4-part stack has tolerances ±0.10, ±0.15, ±0.20, ±0.25 mm. The design permits ±0.60 mm. Decide worst-case vs RSS, and justify against cost.
steps: Worst-case total = 0.10 + 0.15 + 0.20 + 0.25 = 0.70 mm — exceeds the ±0.60 mm allowance, so a worst-case guarantee fails.
Interpretation: the design is fine for high-volume production where part errors are independent and centred — a few assemblies may exceed, at a calculable reject rate.
If every assembly must fit (low volume, safety-critical), you must tighten a tolerance instead.
Cost-optimal fix: tighten only the two LOOSEST contributors (0.20 → 0.15, 0.25 → 0.15), since tight tolerances on already-tight features cost the most per unit of improvement.
example_hard.answer: Worst-case fails (0.70 > 0.60); RSS passes (0.367). Use RSS with a documented reject allowance for volume production, or tighten the two loose contributors if every unit must assemble.

courses.title: Static Modeling of Mechanical Systems (Statics)
courses.blurb: Equilibrium of particles and rigid bodies, trusses, frames, friction, centroids and moments of inertia.

units.title: Vectors & Force Systems
units.summary: Adding, resolving, and taking moments of forces in 2D and 3D.

concepts.d: A force at angle θ: Fx = F cosθ, Fy = F sinθ. Sum components per axis before combining.
F = F·û where û = (dx, dy, dz)/|d|. Use them to write 3D forces cleanly.
A·B = |A||B|cosθ → cosθ = (A·B)/(|A||B|). Used for the angle between a force and an axis.
M = r × F (vector) or M = F·d (scalar, d = perpendicular distance). Sign by convention (CCW positive in 2D).
A couple is two equal, opposite, non-collinear forces — pure moment, no net force. Any force system reduces to one force + one couple at a chosen point.
M = r × F expands to Mx = yFz − zFy, etc. Compute with the determinant.

formulas.e: Fₓ = F cos θ, F_y = F sin θ
formulas.note: θ measured from +x.
Direction θ_R = atan2(R_y, Rₓ).
d = perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action.
r from the moment point to any point on the force's line of action.
Scales to any dimension.

example.problem: Force F = 100 N acts at 30° above the +x axis on a point A = (3, 0) m. Find its moment about the origin.
steps: Components: Fₓ = 100 cos30° = 86.6 N; F_y = 100 sin30° = 50.0 N.
Vector moment about O: M_O = r × F with r = (3, 0).
Check by scalar: perpendicular distance d, M = F·d gives the same value.
example.answer: M_O = 150 N·m counter-clockwise (+z). The horizontal component passes through O and contributes no moment.

traps: Using sin for the wrong axis — always resolve along +x and +y first.
Forgetting the sign convention on moments; state CCW = + before you start.
Using the position vector to a point NOT on the line of action — moment is the same only for points on that line.

practice.q: Two 50 N forces, opposite and 0.4 m apart, act on a beam. What is the resultant force and moment?
practice.a: Resultant force = 0; couple moment = 50 × 0.4 = 20 N·m.

practice.q: Find the angle between A = (2, 1, 0) and B = (0, 1, 2).
Find the moment of F = (30, 40) N acting at point (2, 1) m about the axis through the origin: the z-axis, and then about a vertical line at x = 4 m.
practice.a: About O: M_z = xF_y − yF_x = (2)(40) − (1)(30) = 80 − 30 = 50 N·m (CCW). About x = 4: the perpendicular distance from that line to the line of action changes the reference point to (4, 0): M = (2−4)(40) − (1−0)(30) = −80 − 30 = −110 N·m, i.e. 110 N·m CW.

example_hard.problem: Forces F₁ = 200 N along +x and F₂ = 150 N at 120° from +x both act at the origin. Find the resultant magnitude and direction.
steps: Direction: θ = atan2(129.9, 125) = 46.1° above the +x axis.
Sanity check: the resultant must lie between the two forces (0° and 120°) — 46.1° ✓.
example_hard.answer: R ≈ 180 N at 46° above the +x axis.

units.title: Equilibrium of Particles
units.summary: Forces through a point — the workhorse of cables, springs and pulleys.

concepts.d: Isolate one body, draw EVERY external force (its weight, contact/push, cable tension, spring, reaction), label axes. The FBD is 80% of the mark.
A particle has no rotation: ΣFₓ = 0 and ΣF_y = 0 (add ΣF_z = 0 in 3D). Two equations, two unknowns.
An ideal cable pulls along its length (tension only, never pushes). Over a frictionless pulley, tension is the same on both sides.
F = k·s where s = deformation = L − L₀. Stretch → pull; compression → push, along the spring's axis.
A frictionless contact force is normal (perpendicular) to the surface.

formulas.note: Gives as many equations as there are axes — count unknowns first.
Sign of the force follows the deformation.
g = 9.81 m/s². Mass (kg) ≠ weight (N).

example.problem: A 10 kg sign hangs from two cables: one at 30° and one at 45° to the ceiling. Find both tensions.
steps: FBD at the knot: weight W = 10 × 9.81 = 98.1 N down; T₁ at 30°, T₂ at 45° from the ceiling (up-and-inward).
Vertical (note both cables' vertical components act up): T₁ sin30° + T₂ sin45° = 98.1.
Horizontal: T₁ cos30° = T₂ cos45°.
From the horizontal equation T₂ = T₁ cos30°/cos45° = 1.225·T₁.
example.answer: T₁ (30°) ≈ 71.8 N, T₂ (45°) ≈ 88.0 N. The steeper-from-horizontal cable carries more.

traps: Forgetting the sign that a cable above the load pulls UP (both vertical components positive).
Mixing mass (kg) and weight (N) — multiply by g before balancing forces.
Drawing the FBD of the whole system instead of the isolated knot; unknowns get entangled.

practice.q: A particle is in equilibrium under three forces. One is 30 N east, one is 40 N south. Find the third.
practice.a: Third = −(30 east + 40 south) = 30 N west + 40 N north; magnitude √(30²+40²) = 50 N, at 53.1° north of west.

practice.q: A spring of k = 500 N/m hangs a 2 kg mass. Extension?
A 60 kg crate rests on a frictionless 25° incline held by a rope parallel to the surface. Find the tension and the normal force.

example_hard.problem: A 15 kg lamp hangs from a point where three cables meet: one horizontal to a wall, one at 50° above horizontal to a ceiling, one vertical to the lamp. Find all tensions.
steps: FBD at the knot: weight W = 15 × 9.81 = 147.2 N down; vertical cable tension T_v = W = 147.2 N (it carries the lamp).
Actually the vertical cable IS the lamp's support, so the knot feels 147.2 N down from it. Let T_h = horizontal cable, T_c = ceiling cable at 50°.
Check ΣF_y again with the horizontal cable's zero vertical component ✓.
example_hard.answer: Ceiling cable T_c ≈ 192 N, horizontal cable T_h ≈ 124 N. The steeper the cable, the less horizontal load it must resist.

units.title: Equilibrium of Rigid Bodies
units.summary: When size matters: moments join the force equations.

concepts.d: ΣF = 0 AND ΣM = 0 about any point. That gives 3 equations in 2D (2 force + 1 moment) and 6 in 3D.
Roller (1 unknown, perpendicular), pin/hinge (2 unknowns, any direction), fixed/wall (3 unknowns: two forces + a moment).
A two-force member with no loads between its ends carries equal, opposite, collinear forces. A three-force member's three forces must be concurrent (or parallel).
Replace a distributed load by its resultant (area under the load curve) applied at the centroid of that area — then use point-force methods.
Pick the point where the most unknown lines-of-action pass — it eliminates those unknowns from the equation and saves algebra.

formulas.note: Three equations → three unknowns.
Same about every point — free vector.

formulas.e: R = ∫w(x) dx (or load area), at x̄ = ∫x·w dx / R
formulas.note: For a uniform rectangle: R = w·L at the midpoint.
Six equations, six unknowns.

example.problem: A 6 m uniform beam weighs 200 N. It rests on a pin at the left end (A) and a roller at the right end (B). A 500 N load hangs 2 m from A. Find the reactions.
steps: FBD: at A, Aₓ and A_y; at B a vertical roller reaction B_y; weight 200 N down at 3 m; load 500 N down at 2 m.
No horizontal loads → Aₓ = 0.
example.answer: Aₓ = 0, A_y ≈ 433 N, B_y ≈ 267 N. The load near A loads A more heavily.

traps: Leaving out a support reaction or a distributed load in the FBD.
Forgetting the beam's own weight (uniform → at its midpoint).
Using a moment equation about a point that doesn't eliminate the unknown you're avoiding.

practice.q: How many reaction unknowns does a fixed support add in 2D?
practice.a: Three: a force in x, a force in y, and a moment (couple).

practice.q: Where does the resultant of a triangular distributed load from 0 to w over length L act?
practice.a: At L/3 from the zero end; magnitude = ½·w·L.

practice.q: A three-force member has forces at 0.5 m, 1.5 m and a reaction. If the first two are vertical, what must the third be?
practice.a: The three forces must be concurrent (their lines of action meet at one point) or parallel. Two are vertical hence parallel, so the third must also be vertical — a tilted reaction would violate the three-force concurrency condition.

example_hard.problem: An 8 m beam (weight 300 N, uniform) is pinned at A (left) and supported by a roller at B (right). A triangular distributed load rises from 0 at A to 600 N/m at B. Find the reactions.
steps: Triangular load resultant = ½ × base × height = ½(8)(600) = 2400 N, acting at ⅓ from the tall end, i.e. 8/3 = 2.67 m from B, or 8 − 2.67 = 5.33 m from A.
FBD: A_y and A_x at A, B_y at B, beam weight 300 N down at 4 m, distributed resultant 2400 N down at 5.33 m.
No horizontal loads → A_x = 0.
example_hard.answer: A_y ≈ 951 N, B_y ≈ 1749 N, A_x = 0. The rolling support near the heavy end carries the larger share — always check the moment balance.

units.title: Analysis of Trusses
units.summary: Pin-jointed frameworks — joints and sections.

concepts.d: Members are pin-connected, loads only at joints, members carry axial force only (tension or compression).
Apply ΣF = 0 at each joint in turn; two equations per joint. Start at a joint with ≤ 2 unknowns.
Cut through ≤ 3 members of interest, draw the FBD of one part, apply the 3 equilibrium equations. Fastest when you need just a few members.
A two-member joint with no load/external force → both are zero. A three-member joint with two collinear → the third is zero. Spotting these saves work.
For a planar truss: m + r = 2j for statically determinate (m members, r reactions, j joints). More → over-determinate; fewer → mechanism.

formulas.note: m = members, r = reaction components, j = joints.

formulas.e: Assume members pull away from the joint (+)
formulas.note: Sign is the whole answer — state T or C.

example.problem: A simple triangular truss: joints A (left, pin) and B (right, roller) 4 m apart, apex C 3 m up. A 6 kN load acts down at C. Find the force in each member.
steps: Whole truss: ΣM_A: B_y(4) − 6(2) = 0 → B_y = 3 kN; ΣF_y: A_y = 6 − 3 = 3 kN; Aₓ = 0.
Member lengths: AC = BC = √(2² + 3²) = √13 = 3.606 m.
Joint A: A_y = 3 up. Members AB (horizontal) and AC at angle θ where sinθ = 3/3.606 = 0.832, cosθ = 0.555.
ΣF_y at A: F_AC·sinθ + 3 = 0 → F_AC = −3/0.832 = −3.606 kN (compression).
ΣFₓ at A: F_AB + F_AC·cosθ = 0 → F_AB = 3.606 × 0.555 = 2.0 kN (tension).
By symmetry at B the same magnitudes on the other side; BC = 3.606 kN compression, AB carries 2.0 kN tension.
example.answer: AB = 2.0 kN tension; AC = BC ≈ 3.61 kN compression. Sloped members are in compression under a downward apex load.

traps: Assuming a member is in tension — the sign from equilibrium decides.
Choosing the wrong first joint (start where ≤ 2 unknowns).
Mis-applying zero-force rules at joints that DO carry an external load.

practice.q: A truss has 7 members, 5 joints and 3 reaction components. Determinate?
practice.a: m + r = 7 + 3 = 10; 2j = 10 → determinate.

practice.q: Two non-collinear members meet at an unloaded joint not touching any support. What are their forces?
practice.a: Both are zero-force members.

practice.q: In a truss, a joint has 3 members: two collinear and one perpendicular, with no external load. What is the perpendicular member's force?
practice.a: Zero-force member. The two collinear members balance each other along that axis, and with no external load the perpendicular member has nothing to resist in its direction, so ΣF along it forces F = 0.

example_hard.problem: A Pratt truss spans 8 m with 4 panels of 2 m; a 10 kN load hangs at the centre bottom joint. Use the method of sections to find the force in the middle bottom chord member.
steps: Whole truss: symmetric, so each support carries 5 kN. Reactions A_y = B_y = 5 kN.
Cut vertically through the middle panel, isolating the LEFT half (support A and two joints).
The cut passes through: top chord (compression), a diagonal (tension), and the bottom chord (tension).
Take moments about the top joint where the diagonal and top chord meet — this eliminates both, leaving only the bottom chord force.
The 5 kN reaction at A is 4 m from that top joint; the 10 kN load is 2 m from the centreline at the bottom joint.
ΣM about the top joint: (5 kN)(4 m) − F_bottom(2 m) = 0 → F_bottom = 20/2 = 10 kN.
example_hard.answer: The middle bottom chord carries 10 kN in TENSION. Choosing the moment point to kill two unknowns is the whole trick of the method of sections.

units.title: Frames, Machines & Friction
units.summary: Structures that aren't trusses, and the forces that resist sliding.
